post_text:
We defined strict, conservative SLOs for our core payment API using basic database-backed queue metrics instead of adopting a complex distributed tracing mesh.

The team wanted real-time telemetry, but I pushed for boring, coarse-grained database polling to measure our latency SLIs.

This choice felt incredibly regressive during the planning phase, and I spent sleepless nights wondering if I was holding the team back with outdated patterns.

Everyone else wanted to implement a shiny, reactive event-driven observability platform that promised microsecond-level insights.

I worried my stubbornness would cost us developer velocity and make me look like a dinosaur who feared modern JVM tooling.

Two quarters later, a massive network partition isolated our primary Kubernetes cluster and corrupted the external telemetry collectors.

While the fancy dashboards went completely dark, our simple SQL-based health checks kept reporting accurate queue lag directly to our alerting system.

We shed load gracefully based on those reliable metrics, proving that keeping the telemetry path dead simple was the right choice despite my initial anxiety.

What I learned:

Simple, boring metrics anchored in your primary data store will outlast complex observability pipelines when the system actually starts to fail.
